R_H1.passageTitle: Repairing Together at a Repair Café

passages.label: A
passages.text: Repair Café began at a meeting in Amsterdam in October 2009. Visitors met people who knew how to fix things, and a person who might hesitate to mend a jacket with a familiar designer label could learn how to work on the seam. This gave a consumer a way to keep wearing a jacket without looking for another on the second-hand market.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Today the international organisation's description still emphasises working together. Volunteers provide skills, and tools and materials are available at the meeting, and a consumer takes part in the work whenever possible, rather than simply leaving an object at a counter. Learning is part of the activity, alongside the attempt to repair a possession, and visitors without damaged items can help someone else or read books about repairs while spending time at the meeting.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A repairer and a visitor can collaborate on a practical way to mend a tear, and the design of the garment affects the choice of thread and textile. They may combine a new stitch with fabric from an old item. Some owners admire a unique detail and keep it to preserve a style, and a modest repair can give an individual more confidence to fix another garment at home.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Volunteers do not earn a wage for their labour. Visitors pay for materials, which a repairer may get from a local supplier. The thread can cost little, while learning to place the stitches takes time. Seeing the work gives people one way to think about the working conditions of people who manufacture clothes overseas.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The house rules describe limits too. Experts can refuse certain objects, and help carries no guarantee that an item will work properly at home. Visitors remain responsible for taking away objects that cannot be repaired. The organisers offer an attempt with assistance, rather than a promise that everything brought through the door will be restored.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Busy periods require patience. The international rules limit the initial examination to one broken item per person. Someone with a second item joins the back of the queue again. This arrangement shares available labour and time among visitors. It also explains why bringing several damaged possessions does not provide an immediate place for each one.

passages.label: G
passages.text: Repair Café says that using things longer reduces the volume of raw materials and energy needed to manufacture replacements. Its argument concerns the resources involved in manufacturing, rather than a claim that a particular brand is always environmentally better. Repair also keeps practical skills in use by giving experienced people opportunities to share them.

passages.label: H
passages.text: The organisation is sometimes asked whether it is a competitor of professional repair businesses. It says visitors are often advised to go to professionals. A person who would normally hesitate over an expensive repair can first learn what repair involves. The meeting draws attention to an existing service, while its volunteer help has a different purpose.

R_H2.passageTitle: A Discount for Keeping Clothes in Use

passages.label: A
passages.text: In November 2023, France introduced Refashion’s Repair Bonus for clothing and footwear. It gave consumers a discount on eligible repairs from an approved business. The arrangement mattered whether a garment carried a shop brand or a designer label. Retailers may import clothing or order it from a domestic supplier. But the cost of repair enters the decision later, when an owner has to choose whether to replace it.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The shop takes the discount off the price when the customer pays, and the bill shows how much came off, and Refashion pays the shop back, and this helps the customer pay for work on something they already own. The shop still gets paid for doing the job, while the money goes towards a repair rather than a new item from a clothing shop.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Different repairs are covered. Refashion's published list includes repairing holes, replacing zips and mending seams on clothing. Shoe repairs include work on soles and stitching, and a textile item and a pair of shoes need different practical skills. The scheme recognises that continued use often depends on a small but specific piece of work. In this case it pays for an extra step between manufacturing and disposal.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Approval of the repairer matters as well as the type of repair, and a shop displaying the programme's approval is part of the arrangement for applying the discount and receiving reimbursement. This creates an organised service rather than a general price reduction offered by every clothing supplier, and a familiar brand name alone does not describe participation in that system. An approved repair shop can display advertising for the scheme so that people who hesitate at the full price know about the discount.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Refashion’s 2024 activity report counted more than 550,000 products repaired with the bonus during the year. The total included shoes and clothes, and it measured the volume of work done with the scheme, while changes in the demand for new garments would require a different kind of study.

passages.label: F
passages.text: The report also explained the funding. The Repair Fund and its supporting activities were financed by businesses placing products on the French market. These contributions connected sellers and producers with what happened after products were bought. The arrangement treated the later life of clothing as part of the sector's responsibilities, alongside decisions about how to manufacture and sell new clothes.

passages.label: G
passages.text: People may not know where to find a shop that takes part. Refashion used public events and learning materials in 2024 to promote repair skills and increase participation. This work was separate from the labour of repairing the items. Photographs of a collection can show how repairs convert damaged items into clothes people can wear.

passages.label: H
passages.text: The bonus gives each individual a practical choice about whether to keep a familiar design. Shops can collaborate with local repairers and combine information about price and available services. Someone may admire the style of a unique garment, while a modest reduction in price can increase their confidence that repair is worth trying.

questions.prompt: Which TWO conclusions follow from the article's explanations of what the programme is intended to do and what its figures show?
options: Its figures show how much all owners reduced their spending on replacements.

The reported total is a count of people who will never replace the garments.
Its purpose is to lower the original price of clothes when people buy them.
A separate study would be needed to establish whether demand for newly made clothing changed.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A big brand may outsource the making of clothes to a supplier overseas, and a multinational company can then import the goods and sell them in another market. This use of offshore manufacturing raises a question about the people who do the work, and the label tells a consumer what they bought, but it may say nothing about working conditions. In 2001 the International Labour Organization began to visit clothing factories in Cambodia, and it looked at the hours people worked and how they were paid.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The early reports described both strengths and problems, and the first ILO report found no evidence of child or forced labour in the factories it investigated, but it found difficulties involving overtime payments, hours and discrimination against unions. Those findings referred to the investigated factories, rather than every workplace in the country, and an assessment could identify a specific problem for further action. It was not a guarantee that an entire national manufacturing industry had reached the same standard, or that a good result would remain unchanged.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In 2014 the programme made results for individual factories public on a website. The first reports covered basic rules. They asked about issues such as safe exits and whether factories paid workers for their time. A company that asked a factory to manufacture shirts could now look at the results as well as the quality of the finished goods. The records showed issues at the factories checked, rather than at every factory in the country.

passages.label: D
passages.text: An independent assessment of the programme from 2015 to 2018 reported less overtime without a fall in take-home pay. A buyer might admire a factory’s ability to design quickly, but a good image offers little evidence about an ethical decision. Buyers and suppliers can collaborate and combine wage figures with reports from individual workers, and a modest change can improve conditions without resolving every issue. A practical next step is to focus on the rules and evidence for each factory before judging how much confidence to place in the result.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Following a wage rule and earning enough for a satisfactory life are two different things, and the ILO’s account from 2014 says its checks could answer the first question. Whether people earned enough to live on remained a controversial issue, and a reader can use the reports to find out what changed in the factories that took part. To make sense of a change, it helps to ask which workers were included, when the data were collected and what was still beyond the scope of the study. Imagine two factories where workers take home the same pay each week. If workers at one factory spend fewer hours making clothes, the weekly amount on its own misses a change that could matter to those workers.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: How does the opening relate the company placing an order and the company making it?
options: The seller and supplier must sell under the same label in the same country.
A brand can use a supplier abroad and a company can sell the finished goods in another market.
The company making the goods is described as selling only to its own workers.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What did the ILO look at when it began visiting factories in Cambodia?
options: The relative popularity of brand names
The cost of shipping clothes to stores
How long employees worked and how they were paid

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A buyer argues the first report established that all Cambodian factories avoided forced labour. Which correction does the article support?
options: The finding was about the factories that were investigated.
The report had follow-up inspections at every national manufacturer.
The report proved that overtime was managed correctly at all sites.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What was one pay-related issue identified in the earliest report?
options: How many countries accepted the currency
The same weekly price for different shirts

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: How did access to the inspection findings change what a purchaser could know?
options: A label gave improvements in safety, and the new information added the prices charged in shops.
A label identified the purchase, and the new findings verified the current pay of every individual in the industry.
A label told a purchaser what had been bought, and the new findings could add detail about conditions where it was made.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A buyer reads the later study and says its results answer the question that the earlier wage checks could not. Which assessment is supported?
options: The study reports fewer extra hours without lower earnings, but that still does not say whether the earnings were enough to live on.
Shorter extra hours by themselves show that everyone earned enough to live on.
The study shows that earnings rose enough to settle every question about pay.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why are reports from individual employees useful when read alongside figures?
options: They turn any positive image into proof that the rules were followed.
They add evidence about working conditions to what the pay figures show.
They make the date and scope of the figures irrelevant.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: An inspector confirms a factory paid the amount it was required to pay. How would the article interpret that result?
options: The amount establishes that every household could afford its living costs.
The check establishes that the hours could not be reduced any further.
The check addresses a requirement, while whether the amount meets living costs is a separate question.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A manager shows unchanged weekly earnings as proof that workers' conditions have stayed exactly the same. What does the article suggest asking first?
options: Did the number of hours needed to earn that amount change?
Did the clothing label become better known?
Were both factories using the same supplier for cloth?

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which principle best reflects the article's advice to someone judging the claims about clothing production?
options: If a garment looks well made, assume the workers who made it were treated well.
Check which sites, people and dates the evidence covers, and ask whether it answers the particular claim.
If pay is reported, use the number by itself to conclude that workers can live on it.
